content: The analysis revealed that the homicide rate in Brazil more than doubled during the study period. Despite these efforts, homicides among adolescents and young adults remain a significant public health issue in Brazil, necessitating additional prevention strategies targeting this demographic. Data for the analysis were sourced from Brazil's Mortality Information System, which compiles death certificate information from all states. Additional data for São Paulo city were obtained from the Program for Quality Improvement of Mortality Information. Homicides were defined as deaths caused by intentional injuries inflicted by another person, including legal interventions, and were classified using specific codes from the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) Ninth and Tenth Revisions. Population data for Brazil and São Paulo city were obtained from BGSI, and crude, age-specific, and sex-specific homicide rates were calculated per 100,000 population. To explore the relationship between socioeconomic status and homicide rates in São Paulo city, data on the monthly average income of household heads in all 96 city districts were obtained from the 2000 Brazil Population Census. Pearson correlation analysis was used to assess this association. The findings showed a strong negative correlation between income levels and homicide rates, consistent with research in other urban areas worldwide. This suggests that income inequality and disparities in job and education opportunities may contribute to violence. Further research is needed to better understand this relationship and develop effective interventions. In 2001, the Ministry of Health introduced a national policy to reduce injury-related morbidity and mortality. In 2002, guidelines were issued for health professionals to report child maltreatment. In December 2003, the Brazilian Congress passed a law controlling gun ownership, prohibiting civilians from carrying firearms, and imposing stricter penalties for international firearms trafficking. Plans are also underway to establish an emergency department-based injury registry and an injury surveillance system in São Paulo state to improve data collection and guide policy development. Various violence-prevention initiatives have been launched in Brazil. In Rio de Janeiro, the nongovernmental organization Viva Rio promotes awareness about firearm risks, reduces firearm injuries, fosters peace, and provides vocational training for youth in impoverished communities. In São Paulo state, the São Paulo Institute Against Violence, a coalition of private sector groups, supports violence prevention projects. Additionally, São Paulo city has implemented the Renda Minima Program, offering financial support to low-income families, and the Bolsa Trabalho Program, which promotes youth employment. These programs may help reduce homicide rates, but their impact should be evaluated to inform interventions in other communities. The report acknowledges two limitations. First, death certificate data may underestimate the proportion of firearm-related homicides. Studies in large Brazilian cities, such as Recife, indicate that over 90% of homicides involve firearms, while death certificates report less than 70%. Second, there is limited information on perpetrator characteristics or circumstances of the deaths, such as location, victim-offender relationships, and substance use. A planned homicide surveillance system in São Paulo city aims to integrate data from death certificates, medical examiner records, and police reports to guide public policies. Homicides among adolescents and young adults remain a critical public health issue in Brazil. Additional prevention strategies should involve partnerships among government agencies, universities, the private sector, nongovernmental organizations, and communities. Hypothermia, defined as a core body temperature below 95°F (35°C), is a preventable condition that causes approximately 600 deaths annually in the United States. Modifiable risk factors for hypothermia include alcohol consumption, activity level, and clothing type. Understanding the epidemiology and pathophysiology of hypothermia is essential for prevention. Three cases of fatal hypothermia in 2003 illustrate the condition's risks. In Vermont, a 44-year-old man was found dead outdoors with wet clothing and an elevated blood alcohol concentration (BAC) of 0.30 g/dL. His death was attributed to hypothermia, with alcohol intoxication as a contributing factor. In another Vermont case, a 76-year-old man with Alzheimer's disease was found dead in a swampy area after his car became stuck. His death was caused by hypothermia due to a cold, wet environment. In Alaska, a 35-year-old hiker was found dead in wet and windy conditions with a BAC of 0.28 g/dL and positive toxicology for cocaine and marijuana. His death was attributed to hypothermia, with drug and alcohol intoxication as contributing factors. Certain populations, including alcoholics, drug users, the elderly, the homeless, and individuals with chronic illnesses or preexisting heart disease, are at higher risk of hypothermia-related death. Advanced age, immobility, and medical conditions such as hypothyroidism, congestive heart failure, and diabetes increase vulnerability to hypothermia. Alcohol and drug use exacerbate the risk by impairing judgment, mobility, and thermoregulation. Treatment of hypothermia involves rewarming the patient and providing supportive care, with the method of rewarming depending on the severity of the condition. Even individuals who appear clinically dead may survive with appropriate treatment. Prevention strategies should target high-risk populations and include community programs to check on the elderly, temporary shelters for the homeless, and public health campaigns advising individuals with cardiovascular disease to avoid outdoor activities in cold weather. Alcohol abuse is the third leading preventable cause of death in the United States, contributing to conditions such as cirrhosis, cancer, heart disease, stroke, injury, and depression. Public health efforts aim to reduce binge and heavy drinking, which are associated with these risks. In New Hampshire, a statewide analysis of alcohol use trends from 1991 to 2003 revealed concerning patterns among adolescents and adults. In 2003, 30.6% of adolescents reported binge drinking, defined as consuming five or more drinks on one occasion in the past 30 days. Among adults, 15.8% reported binge drinking in 2001, with men being two to three times more likely than women to engage in this behavior. Women of childbearing age were six times more likely to report binge drinking than women over 45 years old. Heavy drinking, defined as consuming more than two drinks per day for men or more than one drink per day for women, was reported by 6.3% of adults in 2001. Chronic liver disease, a consequence of excessive alcohol use, caused 9.7 deaths per 100,000 New Hampshire residents in 2001. The analysis faced limitations, including underestimation of binge drinking prevalence among current drinkers, lack of weighted data for trend analysis among high school students, and insufficient sample sizes for substate analyses. Additionally, the full burden of alcohol-related health impacts, such as injuries and violence, could not be assessed. Efforts to address alcohol abuse in New Hampshire include annual updates to alcohol surveillance data to guide public health interventions. These programs aim to prevent adolescent drinking and reduce excessive alcohol use among adults.
